title: AIIMS NORCET FON Pattern Mock Test (60 Questions) — ADPIE, Priority, Communication & Ethics
description: 60-question AIIMS NORCET pattern test covering Nursing Process (ADPIE), Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow), Communication in Nursing, and Ethics & Legal Issues with scenario MCQs, MSQs, +1/-0.33 marking, and detailed rationales.
subject: norcet-fon
instructions: AIIMS NORCET Exam Pattern — Fundamentals of Nursing (60 Questions)
Sections: ADPIE (15Q), Priority Settings ABC & Maslow (15Q), Communication (15Q), Ethics & Legal Issues (15Q)
Marking Scheme: +1 mark per correct response | -0.33 negative mark per wrong attempt | 0 for skipped
Hint Coins: 3 Hint Coins credited (5% of 60 questions) — hints stay disabled until clicked

questions.question: The systematic and continuous collection, validation, and organization of patient health data during the nursing process is known as:

options.text: Nursing assessment
Nursing diagnosis
Planning
Evaluation

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET PYQ] Nursing assessment is the first step of the ADPIE nursing process. It involves systematically collecting subjective and objective data, validating accuracy, and clustering cues to form a baseline for clinical judgment.
questions.hint: Think about which step of ADPIE gathers the foundation before any problem can be identified.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A 58-year-old postoperative patient tells the nurse, "My incision feels like it is tearing apart whenever I cough," while the nurse observes a heart rate of 112/min and diaphoresis. How should the nurse classify these findings?

options.text: Both the patient's statement and the vital signs are objective data
Both the patient's statement and the vital signs are subjective data
The patient's statement is subjective data; heart rate and diaphoresis are objective data
The patient's statement is secondary data; heart rate is tertiary data

questions.explanation: Subjective data (symptoms) are covert cues reported directly by the patient (e.g., pain sensation), whereas objective data (signs) are overt, measurable observations gathered by the nurse through senses or instruments (heart rate, sweating).
questions.hint: Distinguish between what the patient feels and reports versus what the nurse can directly measure or see.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: During an abdominal assessment of a patient admitted with suspected bowel obstruction, in which sequence should the nurse perform the physical examination techniques?

options.text: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
Palpation, percussion, inspection, auscultation

questions.explanation: For abdominal assessment, auscultation is performed immediately after inspection and before percussion or palpation. Manipulating the abdomen first can stimulate peristalsis and produce false bowel sounds or increase pain.
questions.hint: Consider which technique must be done before touching the abdomen to avoid altering bowel motility.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which of the following statements are true regarding an ideal nursing care plan? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It should be individualized and patient-centered
It is dynamic and continuously updated based on evaluation
It focuses exclusively on the physician's medical diagnosis
It prioritizes patient needs using clinical frameworks

questions.explanation: [AIIMS NORCET PYQ] A nursing care plan must be patient-centered, individualized, prioritized, and dynamic. Nursing care plans address human responses (nursing diagnoses), not solely the physician's medical diagnosis.
questions.hint: Recall the core characteristics that make a nursing care plan effective across changing patient conditions.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which of the following is a properly written actual (problem-focused) NANDA-I nursing diagnosis using the PES format?

options.text: Myocardial infarction related to coronary artery blockage as evidenced by ECG changes
Impaired gas exchange related to alveolar-capillary membrane changes as evidenced by SpO2 of 86% and dyspnea
Risk for falls related to unsteady gait as evidenced by history of two falls
Acute pain related to appendectomy

questions.explanation: An actual nursing diagnosis uses the three-part PES format: Problem (NANDA label), Etiology ("related to"), and Signs/Symptoms ("as evidenced by"). Myocardial infarction is a medical diagnosis, risk diagnoses do not have "as evidenced by" defining characteristics, and option D lacks defining characteristics.
questions.hint: Check which option uses a nursing label rather than a medical disease and includes all three PES components.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse formulates the diagnosis "Risk for impaired skin integrity related to prolonged immobility." Why does this diagnostic statement omit an "as evidenced by" clause?

options.text: The nurse forgot to complete the physical assessment
Risk diagnoses represent potential problems where defining characteristics are not yet present
NANDA-I no longer requires etiologies or risk factors
Skin integrity cannot be assessed objectively

questions.explanation: Risk nursing diagnoses are two-part statements (Problem + Risk Factors). Because the complication has not occurred yet, there are no current signs or symptoms ("as evidenced by").
questions.hint: Ask yourself whether signs and symptoms can exist for a complication that has not happened yet.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which patient outcome statement best meets the SMART criteria during the planning phase of ADPIE?

options.text: The patient will understand how to inject insulin soon
The patient will feel less anxious during hospitalization
The patient will demonstrate correct subcutaneous insulin self-administration before discharge on day 3
The nurse will teach the patient about diabetic diet every morning

questions.explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound, and they must be written as patient behaviors (not nurse actions). Option C specifies an observable action ("demonstrate") and a clear deadline ("before discharge on day 3").
questions.hint: Look for a measurable patient action paired with a definite timeframe rather than a nurse action or vague verb.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse elevates the head of the bed to 45 degrees and teaches pursed-lip breathing to a patient with COPD without waiting for a physician's order. What type of nursing intervention is this?

options.text: Independent nursing intervention
Dependent nursing intervention
Collaborative nursing intervention
Delegated medical intervention

questions.explanation: Independent (nurse-initiated) interventions are actions within the registered nurse's scope of practice that do not require a provider's prescription, such as positioning, health teaching, and comfort measures.
questions.hint: Consider whether the nurse needed a doctor's prescription to carry out these actions.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A charge nurse is delegating tasks on a busy medical ward. Which tasks can be safely delegated to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel (UAP)? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Measuring routine vital signs of a stable postoperative day-3 patient
Performing the initial admission nursing assessment on a new patient
Assisting a stable stroke patient with a bed bath and linen change
Measuring and recording oral intake and urinary output from a Foley bag

questions.explanation: Under the Five Rights of Delegation, UAPs can perform routine, non-invasive tasks for stable patients (vital signs on stable clients, hygiene, I/O measurement). Initial assessment, nursing diagnosis, teaching, and evaluation require RN clinical judgment and cannot be delegated.
questions.hint: Apply the rule that tasks requiring clinical judgment, assessment, or unstable patient care stay with the RN.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Two hours after administering an oral analgesic, the nurse reassesses the patient's pain score, which dropped from 8/10 to 3/10, and documents that the goal was met. Which phase of ADPIE is the nurse performing?

options.text: Assessment
Diagnosis
Implementation
Evaluation

questions.explanation: Evaluation involves comparing the patient's actual response against the expected outcome criteria to determine whether the goal was met, partially met, or not met, and whether the care plan needs revision.
questions.hint: Focus on the step where the nurse checks if the planned intervention actually achieved the desired patient outcome.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: During shift handoff, a nurse documents a patient's progress using the format: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan, Intervention, Evaluation. Which documentation method is being used?

options.text: DAR (Focus charting)
SOAPIE charting
Charting by Exception (CBE)
Narrative charting

questions.explanation: SOAPIE stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan, Intervention, and Evaluation. It is a problem-oriented medical record (POMR) format closely aligned with the nursing process.
questions.hint: Match the first letters of the six documented components to the acronym.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse reviews a patient's chart and sees a note from the patient's daughter stating that the patient has not been sleeping well at home. What type of data source is the daughter?

options.text: Primary source
Secondary source
Tertiary objective source
Diagnostic source

questions.explanation: The patient is always the primary source of data (unless unconscious or an infant unable to communicate). Family members, caregivers, medical records, and other healthcare professionals are secondary sources.
questions.hint: Remember who holds the status of the primary source in nursing assessment.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A patient with congestive heart failure has a nursing goal: "Patient will ambulate 50 meters without dyspnea by day 2." On day 2, the patient becomes dyspneic after 15 meters. What should the nurse do next in the evaluation phase?

options.text: Discontinue all ambulation permanently
Mark the goal as met because the patient tried
Reassess the patient, identify barriers, and modify the nursing care plan
Discharge the patient with the same plan

questions.explanation: When a goal is not met or only partially met during evaluation, the nursing process cycles back to reassessment to identify contributing factors and revise the care plan accordingly.
questions.hint: Remember that the nursing process is cyclical rather than linear when outcomes are not achieved.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: Which statement best differentiates a nursing diagnosis from a medical diagnosis?

options.text: A nursing diagnosis identifies a specific pathological disease process
A nursing diagnosis focuses on the patient's human response to actual or potential health problems
A nursing diagnosis remains unchanged throughout the patient's hospital stay
A nursing diagnosis can only be written by a nurse practitioner

questions.explanation: Medical diagnoses identify diseases or pathology (e.g., pneumonia) and remain constant until cured, whereas nursing diagnoses describe the individual's response to health conditions (e.g., ineffective airway clearance) and evolve as the patient's status changes.
questions.hint: Think about whether nursing focuses on naming the disease itself or on how the person responds to it.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A patient admitted to the emergency department with severe chest pain and hypotension undergoes a rapid, life-saving evaluation focused strictly on cardiopulmonary stability. What type of nursing assessment is this?

options.text: Initial comprehensive assessment
Time-lapsed assessment
Emergency assessment
Health promotion assessment

questions.explanation: An emergency assessment is performed during a physiological or psychological crisis to rapidly identify life-threatening problems (such as airway obstruction, shock, or cardiac arrest).
questions.hint: Match the urgency and narrow life-saving focus of the scenario to the four types of nursing assessments.
questions.subject: Nursing Process (ADPIE)

questions.question: A nurse is assigned four patients at the start of a morning shift. Which patient should the nurse assess FIRST?

options.text: A stable patient requesting a discharge summary
A patient due for a routine surgical wound dressing change
A postoperative thyroidectomy patient reporting sudden stridor and hoarseness
A diabetic patient asking for guidance on foot care

questions.explanation: Using the ABC framework, stridor and hoarseness after thyroidectomy indicate acute airway obstruction (possibly from hematoma or laryngeal nerve injury). Airway always takes top priority over routine care, education, or administrative requests.
questions.hint: Apply the ABC framework and look for an immediate threat to airway patency.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: According to Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, which patient problem should the nurse address FIRST?

options.text: Social isolation related to prolonged ICU stay
Risk for falls related to sedative medication
Ineffective breathing pattern related to severe asthma exacerbation
Disturbed body image related to recent mastectomy

questions.explanation: Maslow's Hierarchy places physiological needs (oxygenation, airway, circulation, nutrition, elimination) at the base as the highest priority, followed by safety/security, love/belonging, self-esteem, and self-actualization.
questions.hint: Identify which problem threatens a basic physiological survival need at the bottom of Maslow's pyramid.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse finds an adult patient unresponsive, not breathing, and without a palpable carotid pulse in the ward. According to current AHA CPR guidelines, which prioritization sequence should the nurse follow?

options.text: ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation)
CAB (Compressions, Airway, Breathing)
BCA (Breathing, Circulation, Airway)
CBA (Circulation, Breathing, Airway) with rescue breaths first

questions.explanation: While ABC is used for general clinical prioritization in patients with a pulse, AHA BLS/ACLS guidelines mandate the CAB (Compressions, Airway, Breathing) sequence in pulseless cardiac arrest to minimize delay in chest compressions and maintain cerebral/coronary perfusion.
questions.hint: Recall the critical exception where chest compressions take precedence over opening the airway.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with severe COPD whose SpO2 drops to 84% and who is using accessory muscles to breathe. Which action should the nurse perform FIRST?

options.text: Obtain a detailed smoking history from the family
Place the patient in High-Fowler's position and assess airway patency
Document the SpO2 value in the electronic health record
Call the dietitian to adjust caloric intake

questions.explanation: In acute respiratory distress, immediate physiological positioning (High-Fowler's) maximizes lung expansion and eases the work of breathing while assessing airway patency. Documentation and history-taking must wait until the patient is stabilized.
questions.hint: Choose the immediate bedside intervention that directly supports breathing mechanics.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: Which principles guide clinical priority setting in nursing care? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABC) take precedence over non-life-threatening needs
Unstable, acute patients are prioritized over stable, chronic patients
Potential (at-risk) problems always outrank actual physiological problems
Safety and security needs take precedence over self-esteem needs

questions.explanation: Sound clinical prioritization follows ABC, Maslow's hierarchy (physiological > safety > love/belonging > esteem > self-actualization), unstable over stable, acute over chronic, and actual problems before potential/risk problems.
questions.hint: Evaluate each rule against ABC, Maslow's hierarchy, and the actual-versus-potential principle.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: After ensuring that a confused elderly patient's airway, breathing, and vital signs are completely stable, which need becomes the nurse's next priority according to Maslow's framework?

options.text: Encouraging participation in group recreational therapy
Keeping the bed in the lowest position with call bell within reach to prevent falls
Discussing the patient's lifelong career achievements
Assisting the patient to write a personal memoir

questions.explanation: Once physiological needs are met, the second tier of Maslow's hierarchy is Safety and Security. Fall prevention directly addresses physical safety for a confused elderly patient.
questions.hint: Identify the second level of Maslow's pyramid immediately above physiological needs.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: During a mass casualty disaster triage using the START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) system, which patient should be tagged RED (Immediate)?

options.text: A patient with a closed forearm fracture who can walk to the staging area
A patient with an open tibia fracture, respiratory rate 18/min, and capillary refill < 2 seconds
A patient with a respiratory rate of 36/min and radial pulse absent
A patient with massive head trauma, no spontaneous respirations after airway repositioning, and no pulse

questions.explanation: In START triage, RED (Immediate) is assigned to salvageable patients with life-threatening ABC compromise: RR > 30/min, capillary refill > 2 sec (or absent radial pulse), or inability to follow commands. Walking wounded are GREEN, stable fractures are YELLOW, and apneic patients despite airway positioning are BLACK (Expectant).
questions.hint: Recall the RPM (Respirations > 30, Perfusion/pulse absent, Mental status) triggers for the highest-priority triage tag.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse receives shift report on four patients. Which patient requires immediate bedside assessment?

options.text: A patient with chronic COPD whose baseline SpO2 is 90% on 2 L/min nasal cannula
A patient 48 hours post-appendectomy reporting incisional pain of 4/10
A patient with acute pancreatitis whose blood pressure dropped from 124/78 mmHg to 86/52 mmHg with a heart rate of 128/min
A patient with chronic kidney disease scheduled for routine morning hemodialysis

questions.explanation: Acute hypotension and tachycardia in pancreatitis signal hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock (Circulation threat, acute/unstable change). The other patients exhibit expected or stable chronic findings.
questions.hint: Compare expected chronic baselines against a sudden, unstable hemodynamic drop.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient with an anaphylactic reaction to IV ceftriaxone develops wheezing, lip swelling, and a blood pressure of 80/48 mmHg. What is the nurse's FIRST priority action?

options.text: Stop the IV ceftriaxone infusion immediately and maintain airway patency
Complete the hospital medication error incident report
Reassure the family members in the waiting area
Check the patient's serum creatinine level from yesterday

questions.explanation: Stopping the offending allergen immediately prevents further anaphylactic progression while securing the airway and preparing emergency epinephrine (ABC priority).
questions.hint: Think about eliminating the immediate trigger while protecting airway and circulation.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: Which of the following clinical findings represents an UNEXPECTED finding that warrants highest priority over expected postoperative findings?

options.text: Mild serosanguinous drainage on a surgical dressing 6 hours post-op
Drowsiness 1 hour after receiving IV morphine
Sudden onset of unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and acute shortness of breath on post-op day 3
Absence of a bowel movement on post-op day 1

questions.explanation: Unilateral calf swelling with acute dyspnea strongly suggests deep vein thrombosis (DVT) complicated by pulmonary embolism (PE)—a life-threatening ABC emergency. The other findings are expected postoperative responses.
questions.hint: Spot the red-flag complication affecting breathing and circulation rather than normal recovery signs.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient who has just experienced a tonic-clonic seizure. After the jerking stops, the patient is in the postictal phase and breathing noisily with copious oral secretions. What is the priority nursing action?

options.text: Insert a padded tongue blade into the mouth
Turn the patient onto the side (lateral recovery position) to maintain a patent airway
Offer a glass of water to clear the throat
Ask the patient to recall what happened before the seizure

questions.explanation: Placing the postictal patient in the side-lying position promotes drainage of secretions and prevents tongue obstruction or aspiration (Airway priority). Never force anything into the mouth or give oral fluids to a drowsy postictal patient.
questions.hint: Focus on protecting the airway from secretions without causing oral trauma.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: When prioritizing between two patients with physiological needs, which patient should the nurse attend to FIRST?

options.text: A patient who has not had a bowel movement for 3 days
A patient whose chest tube has become disconnected from the water-seal drainage system and is developing dyspnea
A patient requesting lunch because they missed breakfast
A patient complaining of mild dry mouth after surgery

questions.explanation: Even within physiological needs, oxygenation/airway/breathing always outranks nutrition, hydration, and elimination. A disconnected chest tube risks tension pneumothorax and respiratory collapse.
questions.hint: Rank the physiological needs internally by how quickly deprivation becomes fatal.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) has a blood glucose of 480 mg/dL, serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and Kussmaul respirations. Before starting an IV insulin infusion, what is the nurse's priority safety action?

options.text: Administer an oral glucose tablet
Hold insulin and notify the physician regarding the hypokalemia for potassium replacement first
Restrict all IV fluids to prevent overload
Place the patient in Trendelenburg position

questions.explanation: Insulin drives potassium from the extracellular space into cells. Administering insulin when serum potassium is < 3.3 mEq/L can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias (Circulation priority). Potassium must be corrected before insulin infusion.
questions.hint: Remember what IV insulin does to serum potassium levels and the resulting cardiac risk.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A nurse is planning care for a newly diagnosed breast cancer patient who says, "I feel ugly and I am sure my husband will leave me." According to Maslow's Hierarchy, which level of need is this patient expressing?

options.text: Physiological need
Safety and security need
Love, belonging, and self-esteem needs
Self-actualization need

questions.explanation: Concerns about altered body image reflect self-esteem needs, while fear of rejection by a spouse reflects love and belonging needs—both sitting above physiological and safety tiers in Maslow's hierarchy.
questions.hint: Match body-image distress and relationship fears to the middle tiers of Maslow's pyramid.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: A patient admitted with severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding has hematemesis, cold clammy skin, BP 78/46 mmHg, and HR 134/min. Which nursing intervention is the highest priority?

options.text: Obtain a comprehensive dietary history
Educate the patient on avoiding NSAIDs after discharge
Establish large-bore IV access and initiate prescribed fluid resuscitation while monitoring airway
Schedule a follow-up outpatient endoscopy appointment

questions.explanation: Active hemorrhagic shock is a life-threatening Circulation (and Airway, due to hematemesis) emergency. Establishing large-bore IV access for rapid volume resuscitation while protecting the airway is the top priority.
questions.hint: Identify the immediate life-saving intervention for active hemorrhagic shock.
questions.subject: Priority Settings (ABC & Maslow)

questions.question: Which therapeutic communication technique involves directing ideas, feelings, questions, or content back to the client so they can explore their own thoughts and emotions?

options.text: Probing
Clarifying
Reflecting
Challenging

questions.explanation: [NORCET-6 Mains PYQ] Reflecting mirrors the client's feelings, ideas, or questions back to them (e.g., "It sounds like you feel overwhelmed by this diagnosis"), demonstrating empathy and encouraging self-exploration. Probing and challenging are non-therapeutic, while clarifying seeks the nurse's understanding of an unclear message.
questions.hint: Think of a mirror that returns the patient's own emotions and ideas for self-exploration.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A preoperative patient says, "I am terrified that I will not wake up from anesthesia." Which response by the nurse demonstrates therapeutic communication?

options.text: "Don't worry, our anesthesiologist is the best in the city; everything will be fine."
"Why are you so scared? Thousands of people have this surgery every day."
"It sounds like you are feeling very anxious about the anesthesia. Tell me more about what worries you most."
"Let's talk about what you plan to eat after the surgery instead."

questions.explanation: Option C uses reflecting and exploring (open-ended invitation) to validate feelings and invite discussion. Option A gives false reassurance, Option B asks a judgmental "Why?" and belittles fear, and Option D changes the subject—all non-therapeutic barriers.
questions.hint: Look for the response that validates the emotion and invites the patient to talk rather than shutting down the conversation.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: According to Hildegard Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory, during which phase of the nurse-patient relationship do the nurse and patient first meet, establish trust, and clarify roles and expectations?

options.text: Pre-interaction phase
Orientation phase
Working phase
Termination phase

questions.explanation: Peplau's four phases are: Pre-interaction (self-examination and chart review before meeting), Orientation (initial meeting, building trust, defining roles and problem), Working (active problem-solving and interventions), and Termination (closure and discharge planning).
questions.hint: Recall which phase marks the very first face-to-face meeting where rapport and contract parameters are set.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse is calling an on-call physician to report a sudden drop in a patient's urine output and blood pressure. Using the SBAR handoff tool, what information should the nurse state under "B" (Background)?

options.text: "The patient's current BP is 84/50 mmHg and urine output is 10 mL/hr."
"The patient is a 65-year-old male admitted yesterday for septic shock, allergic to penicillin, on IV ceftriaxone."
"I think the patient is developing worsening hypoperfusion."
"Would you like to order a 500 mL normal saline bolus and come assess him?"

questions.explanation: In SBAR: Situation = current urgent problem; Background = pertinent clinical history, admission diagnosis, medications, allergies; Assessment = nurse's clinical impression/findings; Recommendation = specific action requested.
questions.hint: Distinguish relevant past clinical context from the immediate reason for the call or the nurse's request.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of NON-THERAPEUTIC communication techniques that block effective nurse-patient interaction? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Giving false reassurance ("Everything will be completely fine.")
Asking "Why?" questions that put the patient on the defensive
Using purposeful silence to allow the patient to gather thoughts
Giving personal advice ("If I were you, I would definitely choose surgery.")

questions.explanation: False reassurance, "Why?" questions, and giving personal advice block therapeutic communication by invalidating feelings, inducing defensiveness, or undermining patient autonomy. Purposeful silence is a therapeutic technique.
questions.hint: Identify the three responses that either dismiss feelings, create defensiveness, or take away patient decision-making.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A nurse sits squarely facing a grieving patient, maintains an open posture, leans slightly forward, keeps appropriate eye contact, and stays relaxed. Which active-listening framework is the nurse demonstrating?

options.text: SBAR
SOLER
ADPIE
SOAPIE

questions.explanation: Egan's SOLER acronym guides therapeutic non-verbal active listening: Sit squarely facing the client, Open posture, Lean toward the client, Eye contact (culturally appropriate), and Relax.
questions.hint: Match the five non-verbal body-language cues to the five-letter active listening acronym.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient who speaks only Bengali is admitted for an emergency procedure, and the nurse speaks only English and Hindi. The patient's 10-year-old son offers to translate the surgical risks. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Allow the 10-year-old son to translate because he is readily available
Use hand gestures and proceed without translation
Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter to facilitate accurate communication
Ask a housekeeping staff member who speaks Bengali to explain the surgical risks

questions.explanation: Using minor children or untrained staff as medical interpreters risks inaccurate translation, breaches confidentiality, and places emotional burden on the child. A trained medical interpreter ensures accuracy and legal validity.
questions.hint: Consider who is legally and clinically qualified to translate complex medical information accurately.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: When communicating with an older adult who has presbycusis (age-related sensorineural hearing loss), which nursing approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Shout loudly into the patient's ear from behind
Face the patient in good lighting, speak clearly in a lower-pitched tone, and reduce background noise
Speak very rapidly in a high-pitched voice
Cover your mouth while speaking to prevent droplet spread

questions.explanation: Presbycusis primarily impairs high-frequency hearing. Facing the patient allows lip-reading and facial cues, while speaking clearly at a normal-to-lower pitch in a quiet, well-lit room optimizes comprehension. Shouting distorts sound and raises pitch.
questions.hint: Remember which sound frequencies are lost first in age-related hearing loss and how visual cues help.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient with expressive (Broca's) aphasia following a left-hemisphere stroke understands questions but struggles to form spoken words. How should the nurse communicate with this patient?

options.text: Finish every sentence quickly for the patient to save time
Speak to the patient as if they cannot understand anything
Ask simple yes/no questions, allow extra time to respond, and provide a communication board
Avoid asking the patient any questions to prevent frustration

questions.explanation: Patients with expressive (Broca's) aphasia have intact comprehension but impaired speech production. Asking simple yes/no questions, giving unhurried time, and using picture/letter boards respect dignity and facilitate communication.
questions.hint: Keep in mind that comprehension is intact even though word production is difficult.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: During a counseling session, a patient says, "I don't think my medications are working at all." The nurse replies, "You feel that your medications are not helping you?" Which therapeutic communication technique is the nurse using?

options.text: Restating
Giving advice
Probing
Challenging

questions.explanation: Restating (paraphrasing) repeats the main idea the patient expressed in slightly different words to confirm understanding and encourage further elaboration.
questions.hint: Notice how the nurse echoes the core content of the patient's statement back to verify meaning.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: In proxemics (use of personal space in communication), which spatial zone is typically used by a nurse during a routine bedside interview or health teaching with a patient?

options.text: Intimate zone (0 to 18 inches)
Personal zone (18 inches to 4 feet)
Social zone (4 to 12 feet)
Public zone (greater than 12 feet)

questions.explanation: Hall's proxemics zones: Intimate (0–18 in) is used for physical procedures/assessments; Personal (18 in–4 ft) is ideal for bedside interviews, counseling, and teaching; Social (4–12 ft) is used for rounds or group discussions; Public (>12 ft) is for lectures.
questions.hint: Recall the distance range comfortable for one-on-one conversation without invading intimate physical space.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A physician gives an urgent telephone order for a medication dose during a night shift. What is the nurse's priority communication action to ensure patient safety?

options.text: Memorize the order and administer it immediately before writing it down
Write down the order verbatim and perform a complete "read-back" verification with the physician
Ask a colleague to listen on speakerphone without writing it down
Wait until morning rounds to clarify the dose

questions.explanation: Joint Commission and hospital safety protocols mandate "write-down and read-back" (TORB — Telephone Order Read-Back) for all verbal/telephone orders to prevent medication errors from sound-alike drug names or misheard doses.
questions.hint: Think of the standard two-step safety verification required for every telephone prescription.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: During which phase of the nurse-patient relationship should the nurse begin preparing the patient for discharge and termination of the therapeutic relationship?

options.text: Only on the exact morning of discharge
During the orientation phase and reinforced throughout the working phase
During the pre-interaction phase before meeting the patient
Termination should never be discussed to avoid upsetting the patient

questions.explanation: Effective termination planning begins as early as the orientation phase (by clarifying the time-limited nature of the relationship) and is reinforced during the working phase so the patient can transition smoothly without feelings of abandonment.
questions.hint: Consider when setting clear expectations about the end of care prevents sudden separation distress.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: A patient says, "The nurses here never listen to me and don't care about my pain." Which response by the nurse is NON-THERAPEUTIC because it is defensive?

options.text: "It sounds like you are feeling unheard about your pain."
"That's not true—everyone on this ward works very hard to take good care of you."
"Can you tell me more about what happened when you asked for pain relief?"
"Let's review your pain management plan together right now."

questions.explanation: Defending (Option B) protects staff/hospital reputation rather than addressing the patient's distress, which shuts down trust and invalidates the patient's experience.
questions.hint: Spot the response that argues back to protect the nursing team instead of exploring the patient's concern.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question: Which element of the communication process confirms whether the receiver accurately understood the sender's message?

options.text: Channel
Encoding
Feedback
Referent

questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's verbal or non-verbal response back to the sender, closing the communication loop and verifying whether the message was understood as intended.
questions.hint: Identify the return signal that tells the sender the message got through accurately.
questions.subject: Communication in Nursing

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A nurse obtains the patient's signature on the surgical consent form.
Reason (R): A nurse is legally authorized to obtain informed consent from the patient.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: [NORCET-10 Prelims PYQ] A nurse may witness the patient's signature on the consent form (so A is true), but the legal responsibility to explain risks, benefits, and alternatives and obtain informed consent belongs strictly to the performing physician/surgeon (so R is false).
questions.hint: Separate the procedural act of witnessing a signature from the legal duty of explaining the procedure.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse did not administer a scheduled dose of IV antibiotic but signed the Medication Administration Record (MAR) indicating that it was given. This action represents which legal/ethical breach?

options.text: Malpractice (and falsification of legal records)
Beneficence
Assault
Battery

questions.explanation: [NORCET-10 Mains PYQ] Failing to administer prescribed medication and falsifying the legal medical record is a serious breach of professional standards of care constituting malpractice/professional misconduct. Assault is a threat, battery is unwanted touching, and beneficence is an ethical principle meaning "doing good."
questions.hint: Eliminate ethical principles and intentional physical-contact torts to identify the professional breach of care.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A competent adult patient refuses a life-saving blood transfusion based on religious beliefs. The nurse respects the patient's decision and notifies the physician. Which ethical principle is the nurse upholding?

options.text: Autonomy
Non-maleficence
Fidelity
Veracity

questions.explanation: Autonomy is the ethical principle of self-determination—recognizing a competent individual's right to make independent decisions regarding their own healthcare, including the right to refuse treatment.
questions.hint: Think of the ethical principle rooted in self-governance and personal decision-making rights.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse tells an agitated patient, "If you do not lie still right now, I will tie you to the bed and give you a painful injection." The nurse does not touch the patient. Which intentional tort has the nurse committed?

options.text: Assault
Battery
Negligence
Libel

questions.explanation: Assault is an intentional tort involving a verbal or physical threat that places a person in reasonable fear or apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact, even without actual touching.
questions.hint: Distinguish between the threat of unwanted contact and the actual physical act of touching.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse administers an intramuscular sedative to a competent, refusing patient without consent or legal emergency authorization. Which intentional tort has occurred?

options.text: Assault
Battery
Slander
Malpractice

questions.explanation: Battery is the intentional, unconsented harmful or offensive physical touching of another person—even if the healthcare provider believes the treatment is beneficial.
questions.hint: Identify the intentional tort defined specifically by unauthorized physical contact.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: Which four elements must be proven in court to establish a legal claim of nursing malpractice? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Duty of care owed to the patient
Breach of the standard of care
Causation linking the breach to the injury
Actual harm or damages suffered by the patient

questions.explanation: All four elements—Duty, Breach of duty, Causation (foreseeability/proximate cause), and Damages (actual harm)—must be proven by the plaintiff to establish malpractice (professional negligence).
questions.hint: Recall the classic four-link legal chain required to prove professional negligence.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: An ethical principle that obligates a nurse to tell the truth and never intentionally deceive a patient or family is called:

options.text: Fidelity
Justice
Veracity
Beneficence

questions.explanation: [Nursing Officer PYQ] Veracity means truthfulness and honesty in all professional interactions. Fidelity means keeping promises, justice means fairness, and beneficence means doing good.
questions.hint: Connect the Latin root "verus" (true) to the corresponding ethical principle.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse promises a postoperative patient, "I will return in 15 minutes with your pain medication," and returns promptly at 15 minutes as promised. Which ethical principle is demonstrated?

options.text: Justice
Fidelity
Non-maleficence
Autonomy

questions.explanation: [Nursing Officer PYQ] Fidelity refers to faithfulness, loyalty, and honoring commitments or promises made to patients.
questions.hint: Think of the principle associated with keeping one's word and being faithful to commitments.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse accidentally administers double the prescribed dose of insulin to a patient, immediately monitors blood glucose, notifies the physician, and completes an incident report. What should the nurse document in the patient's medical chart?

options.text: "An incident report was completed and sent to risk management."
"Nurse made a severe medication error due to short staffing."
Objective clinical facts: exact dose given, time, blood glucose readings, physician notification, and interventions taken
Nothing, to avoid legal liability

questions.explanation: An incident (occurrence) report is an internal quality-improvement/risk-management document and must NEVER be mentioned in the patient's chart. The chart must contain only objective clinical facts, patient response, provider notification, and corrective actions.
questions.hint: Remember the strict legal rule separating internal risk-management reports from the patient's medical record.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse posts a photograph of a patient's rare surgical wound on social media without the patient's permission, even though the patient's face is cropped out, and the patient is identifiable by a unique tattoo. Which legal violation has occurred?

options.text: Assault
Invasion of privacy and breach of confidentiality
False imprisonment
Beneficence

questions.explanation: Sharing identifiable patient images or health information without authorization violates patient confidentiality and constitutes the intentional tort of invasion of privacy.
questions.hint: Consider which right is violated when private medical details or identifiable photos are shared publicly.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: In which year did the Indian Nursing Council (INC) publish the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct for Nurses in India?
questions.explanation: [Nursing Officer PYQ] The Indian Nursing Council (INC) adopted and published the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct for Nurses in India in 2006 to guide ethical accountability and professional standards nationwide.
questions.hint: Recall the mid-2000s milestone year when INC formalized India's nursing ethics code.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A competent patient decides to leave the hospital Against Medical Advice (AMA). The nurse locks the ward door and confiscates the patient's clothes to prevent them from leaving. Which tort has the nurse committed?

options.text: Defamation
False imprisonment
Negligence
Slander

questions.explanation: Preventing a competent adult from leaving a healthcare facility without legal authority (or applying unjustified physical/chemical restraints) constitutes false imprisonment. The proper action is to explain risks, notify the physician, and ask the patient to sign an AMA form.
questions.hint: Identify the intentional tort involving unlawful restriction of a person's freedom of movement.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse is dining at a restaurant when a patron collapses with choking. The nurse performs the Heimlich maneuver within their scope of training without expecting compensation. Which legal principle protects the nurse from ordinary negligence liability in this emergency?

options.text: Respondeat superior
Good Samaritan Law
Res ipsa loquitur
Informed consent doctrine

questions.explanation: Good Samaritan laws protect healthcare professionals and bystanders who render voluntary, good-faith emergency care at the scene of an accident/emergency without gross negligence or expectation of payment.
questions.hint: Think of the legal protection named after a biblical parable for voluntary emergency aid.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: During a crowded triage shift, a nurse ensures that all patients receive fair, equitable care based on clinical urgency regardless of socioeconomic status, caste, or ability to pay. Which ethical principle is applied?

options.text: Justice
Veracity
Fidelity
Non-maleficence

questions.explanation: Justice requires fairness and equitable distribution of healthcare resources without discrimination.
questions.hint: Match fairness and impartial allocation of care to the corresponding ethical principle.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues

questions.question: A nurse writes a false, malicious statement in a colleague's public evaluation accusing them of stealing narcotics without any evidence, damaging the colleague's reputation. This written defamation is legally termed:

options.text: Slander
Libel
Battery
Fraud

questions.explanation: Defamation of character has two forms: Libel (written or published false statements that harm reputation) and Slander (spoken false statements).
questions.hint: Distinguish between spoken defamation and written/published defamation.
questions.subject: Ethics & Legal Issues
